6690:
Fundamentalism is the strong, unwavering belief that a particular set of core principles — usually from a religion or ideology — must be followed exactly as they were originally stated, without any change, reinterpretation, or compromise, regardless of how the world changes around them.

Think of it this way: imagine a rulebook written hundreds of years ago. A fundamentalist believes that rulebook must be followed word for word, forever, and that any attempt to update, adapt, or reread it in a modern context is wrong, dangerous, or even sinful.
The word "fundamentalism" can apply to religion, politics, and even certain ideologies. However, it is most commonly used in the context of religion.

This is where the term is used the most. Religious fundamentalism means a strict, literal belief in the sacred texts of a religion — like the Bible, the Quran, or the Torah — and a rejection of any modern interpretation that softens, questions, or changes those texts.

A religious fundamentalist believes:

  • Their holy scripture is 100% literally true.
  • The original rules and laws laid down in that text must govern life today, just as they did centuries ago.
  • Modernism, secularism, and liberal thinking are threats to their faith.
  • There is no room for doubt, debate, or flexible interpretation.

For example, a Christian fundamentalist might insist that the Earth was created in exactly six days, exactly as described in the Bible — not as a metaphor, not as a poetic story, but as a literal fact. A Islamic fundamentalist might insist that all laws of society must come directly and strictly from the Quran and early Islamic legal tradition, with no influence from modern democratic or secular thinking.

It is important to note that fundamentalism exists across virtually all major world religions — Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Sikhism, and others all have fundamentalist movements within them.

No matter which religion or ideology it appears in, fundamentalism tends to share certain defining features:

1. Literalism. The text means exactly what it says. No metaphor, no context, no reinterpretation. If the text says the Earth is flat, a fundamentalist believes the Earth is flat.

2. Absolutism. There is only one truth — theirs. Other views are not just different; they are wrong, corrupt, or evil.

3. Resistance to change. The modern world, with its evolving values and new scientific discoveries, is seen as a corrupting force. The fundamentalist wants to hold the line firmly against it.

4. A sense of threat. Fundamentalism often intensifies when a group feels that its beliefs, culture, or identity are under attack. It is frequently a reaction — a pushback against liberalism, modernity, or outside influence.

5. Clear in-group vs. out-group thinking. "We are the true believers. Everyone else has gone astray." This sharp division between "us" (the pure, faithful) and "them" (the corrupt, the lost) is a hallmark of fundamentalist thinking.

6. Authority of the original source. Whether it is a holy book, a founding document, or an ancient tradition, fundamentalists treat their original source of truth as the highest possible authority — above science, above courts, above modern governments.

This is crucial to understand: fundamentalism does not automatically mean violence or terrorism. This is one of the biggest misconceptions about the word.

Many fundamentalists are peaceful, law-abiding people who simply live by very strict religious rules, keep to their own communities, avoid outside influences, and raise their families according to their beliefs. They might refuse to watch television, send their children to secular schools, or socialise with outsiders — but they do not harm anyone.

On the other end of the spectrum, some fundamentalist movements do become extreme and dangerous. When fundamentalist beliefs combine with political power and a willingness to use force, they can lead to violence, terrorism, or oppressive regimes. But this is the extreme end — not the definition of fundamentalism itself.

Think of fundamentalism as a sliding scale:

Strict but peaceful private observance → Social separatism → Political activism → Militant extremism

The word "fundamentalism" covers a wide portion of that scale, but it does not automatically land at the violent end.
How Fundamentalism Differs from Similar Words

Since you want to understand this fully, it helps to compare it to nearby ideas so you can see exactly where fundamentalism sits:

Orthodoxy means strictly following the traditional, accepted beliefs of a religion. It is about staying true to established doctrine. Orthodoxy is normal and widely accepted within many religions. Fundamentalism goes further — it is more rigid, more defensive, more reactive, and more likely to view the outside world as an enemy.

Conservatism (in a religious sense) means preferring traditional practices over new ones. A conservative believer might resist change but is often open to some adjustment over time. A fundamentalist typically rejects any adjustment at all.

Radicalism means pushing for extreme or revolutionary change — it can be in any direction. Fundamentalism is usually anti-change, so while some fundamentalists can become radical (especially politically), the words are not synonyms.

Extremism refers to holding views that are far outside the mainstream, often combined with a willingness to take extreme actions. Not all fundamentalists are extremists. But when fundamentalism crosses into violence or hatred, it enters the territory of extremism.

The word has also been stretched to apply outside religion when someone follows a non-religious ideology with the same rigid, uncompromising, all-or-nothing intensity.

For instance:

  • Market fundamentalism refers to the absolute belief that free markets must never be regulated or interfered with — that the market is always right, no exceptions. (This is also called laissez-faire thinking taken to its extreme.)
  • Political fundamentalism refers to rigidly following a political ideology as if it were sacred scripture, refusing to compromise, question, or update it.

In these non-religious uses, the word carries the same core meaning: uncompromising, rigid adherence to a set of core beliefs as though they are absolute and beyond question.

Understanding why it happens helps you understand it more deeply.

Fundamentalism typically emerges when a community feels:

  • Threatened — by modernisation, secularism, foreign cultures, or political change.
  • Lost — when rapid social change leaves people without a clear sense of identity or moral order.
  • Disrespected — when a group feels its beliefs are being mocked, marginalised, or eroded.

In this sense, fundamentalism is often a defensive reaction — a way of drawing a firm line in the sand and saying, "This is who we are. This is what we believe. And we will not let it be taken from us."

If you had to explain "fundamentalism" in three sentences to someone:

Fundamentalism is the belief that the original, core rules of a religion or ideology must be followed exactly and without change, no matter what the modern world says. Fundamentalists treat their founding texts or principles as absolute, perfect truth — not open to reinterpretation. It is a rigid, uncompromising way of thinking that often arises when people feel their beliefs or identity are under threat.
6691:
A fundamentalist is a person who believes in a strict, literal, and completely uncompromising reading of the core principles of a belief system — and refuses to water them down, reinterpret them, or allow them to be changed, no matter what.

Think of it this way: most people, over time, adjust their beliefs slightly as the world changes around them. A fundamentalist is the person who says, "No. The original rules are the rules. Forever. Full stop."

The word was born in a religious context, and this is still its primary and most common meaning.

Every major religion has a founding text — the Bible for Christians, the Quran for Muslims, the Torah for Jews, and so on. These texts were written a very long time ago. Over centuries, many religious people began interpreting these texts in ways that fit the modern world — sometimes reading passages as metaphors, sometimes accepting that certain rules no longer apply literally today.

A religious fundamentalist rejects all of that. They believe:

  • The sacred text must be taken literally, word for word, exactly as written.
  • It is eternally true and needs no reinterpretation or updating.
  • Adapting it to fit modern life is a form of corruption or betrayal of the faith.
  • Their interpretation is the only correct one, and all other versions are wrong.

For example, a Christian fundamentalist might insist that the Earth was created by God in exactly six days, exactly as the Book of Genesis states, and reject the scientific theory of evolution entirely — not because they haven't heard of it, but because they believe the Bible's account is the absolute, literal truth.
The Three Key Traits of a Fundamentalist

No matter the religion or belief system, a fundamentalist is almost always defined by these three things:

1. Literalism — They read their founding text exactly as written, with no room for metaphor, allegory, or symbolic interpretation.

2. Inerrancy — They believe the founding text is perfectly, completely, and permanently true. It cannot be wrong. It cannot be outdated.

3. Non-negotiability — They will not compromise, adapt, or soften their beliefs to get along with others or to fit changing times. This is the defining characteristic. A fundamentalist doesn't say, "Well, perhaps we need to rethink this in a modern context." They say, "This is the truth. The world must adjust to it, not the other way around."
Beyond Religion: The Wider Use of the Word

Today, the word has escaped its religious origins and is applied to almost any belief system. You will often hear phrases like:

  • "Free-market fundamentalist" — Someone who believes, with total and unwavering conviction, that markets should never be regulated by governments. Any suggestion of regulation, no matter how small, is unacceptable to them.
  • "Ideological fundamentalist" — Someone who follows a political ideology so rigidly that they refuse to acknowledge any flaw in it or any merit in opposing ideas.

The common thread, in all cases, is the same: absolute, inflexible devotion to a core set of beliefs, with zero willingness to question or compromise them.

It is very important to distinguish a fundamentalist from someone who is simply deeply religious or deeply committed to a cause, because people often confuse the two.

  • A devout person can be deeply faithful, pray every day, and follow their religion's rules carefully — and still be open to modern interpretation, dialogue, or nuance. They are not a fundamentalist.
  • An orthodox believer follows traditional practices strictly but may still acknowledge that some texts can be read in more than one way. They are not necessarily a fundamentalist.
  • A fundamentalist, by contrast, draws a hard, unmovable line: this text means exactly this, and I will never entertain any other reading of it.

The key test is: Is this person open to any reinterpretation or reconsideration of their core beliefs? If the answer is an absolute no, you are looking at a fundamentalist.
Does the Word Have a Negative Tone?

Yes, in modern everyday usage, calling someone a "fundamentalist" usually carries a critical or negative tone. It implies the person is:

  • Rigid — unable or unwilling to think flexibly.
  • Intolerant — dismissive of any viewpoint that differs from their own.
  • Extreme — in the degree of their conviction.

However — and this is important — fundamentalists themselves do not see their position as negative at all. From their own perspective, they are simply being faithful, honest, and principled. They see themselves as courageous guardians of a great truth, standing firm while others around them weaken and compromise.

So the word works in two directions: from the outside, it is often an accusation; from the inside, it can be a badge of honour.

These two words are often used together, and they overlap — but they are not the same thing.

  • All extremists are fundamentalists (they hold absolute, uncompromising beliefs).
  • But not all fundamentalists are extremists in the sense of using or supporting violence.

A fundamentalist may simply live quietly according to their strict beliefs, avoiding anyone who thinks differently. An extremist goes further — they may believe the system of beliefs justifies aggressive or even violent action against those who disagree. The distinction matters.

A fundamentalist is a person who holds strictly and absolutely to the original, literal principles of a religion or ideology, refuses any modern reinterpretation, sees those principles as permanently and perfectly true, and will not compromise on them under any circumstances. The word is most commonly used in religious contexts but applies to any field of belief. In everyday usage, it usually implies criticism of someone's inflexibility — though the person so described would rarely agree with that criticism.
6692: "Funerary" is an adjective that means relating to, used for, or associated with death, burial, and the rituals around them. When you place this word in front of a noun, you're saying that noun has a connection to how people deal with the dead — the ceremonies, the objects, the structures, and the traditions surrounding death and burial.

The word "funerary" is almost always used to modify a noun. Here are the most common combinations, each explained:

  • Funerary rites / rituals — The ceremonies performed when someone dies. This includes things like washing the body, prayers, processions, and burial customs. Every culture throughout history has had funerary rites.
  • Funerary objects / artifacts — Items placed with or near a dead person, often inside a tomb or grave. In ancient Egypt, for example, archaeologists have found funerary objects like jars, amulets, and food offerings buried alongside the dead.
  • Funerary art — Art created specifically in connection with death and burial. Decorated coffins, carved sarcophagi, painted tomb walls, and sculpted grave markers are all examples of funerary art.
  • Funerary architecture — Structures built for the dead. Pyramids, mausoleums, tombs, catacombs, and crypts are all funerary architecture — they exist because of death, not for the living.
  • Funerary monument — A structure built to honor and commemorate someone who has died. Think of grand tombs or elaborate grave markers.
  • Funerary mask — A mask made to cover the face of a dead person, often crafted to resemble their face. The famous golden mask of Pharaoh Tutankhamun is one of the most well-known funerary masks in the world.
  • Funerary practices — The broader customs, habits, and traditions a culture follows when dealing with death and the dead. This is a wide term covering everything from how a body is prepared to how mourners are expected to behave.
The tone and register of this word

"Funerary" is a formal and scholarly word. You will encounter it most often in:

  • Academic writing — history, archaeology, anthropology, and religious studies
  • Museum labels and descriptions — "This gallery contains funerary objects from ancient Mesopotamia."
  • Historical and archaeological contexts — when discussing ancient or past civilizations and how they handled death

You would not typically use "funerary" in casual everyday conversation. Nobody says, "I attended a funerary ceremony yesterday." In everyday speech, you'd just say "funeral." The word "funerary" signals a certain seriousness and distance — it's the kind of word that steps back and examines something analytically rather than personally.
How it differs from "funeral" used as an adjective

Both "funeral" and "funerary" can describe things related to death and burial, and they overlap significantly. However, there are clear differences in how they're used:

  • "Funeral" (as an adjective) is more casual and refers directly to the event of a funeral. Examples: funeral home, funeral procession, funeral service, funeral flowers. These are things belonging to or used at a specific funeral event.
  • "Funerary" is broader and more formal. It doesn't just refer to a single funeral event — it refers to the entire world of death-related customs, objects, and structures. You'd use "funerary" when discussing ancient civilizations, historical practices, or archaeological finds, where you're talking about a whole category of behavior and material culture around death, not just one event.

So: a "funeral speech" is the speech given at a specific funeral. "Funerary inscriptions" refers to the broader tradition of writing things on tombs and grave markers across history and cultures.

In short, "funeral" is the everyday word; "funerary" is the formal, scholarly, broader version.

• "The archaeologists uncovered a chamber full of funerary goods, including painted pottery and bronze weapons placed beside the skeleton."
  • "Ancient Egyptian funerary practices were deeply connected to their beliefs about the afterlife."
  • "The pyramid at Giza is the most famous funerary structure ever built."
  • "Funerary art from the Roman period reveals how people of that era thought about death and memory."
  • "The museum's funerary collection spans thousands of years and dozens of cultures."

If you see the word "funerary" before any noun, ask yourself: does this thing exist because of death, or is it used in connection with burying and honoring the dead? If yes, "funerary" is the right descriptor. It's a formal, precise adjective that belongs to the world of tombs, burial customs, death rituals, and the objects and structures that humans have created around the fact of dying.
6693:
Funereal means having the feel, mood, or atmosphere of a funeral.

That's the heart of it. When you call something funereal, you are saying it carries the same heavy, dark, solemn, mournful quality that surrounds a funeral — even if no one has actually died and there is no actual funeral happening.

Think about what a funeral feels like. People speak in hushed, careful voices. The mood is thick and heavy with grief. No one is laughing. Everything moves slowly. There is a suffocating sense of sadness pressing down on the room. Colors are dark. Silence feels loud.

When something is funereal, it replicates that feeling — in a room, in a person's face, in music, in the way someone walks, in the air of a place. The word is almost always used in this transferred, metaphorical way, not to describe an actual funeral.
What Makes It Different From Just "Sad"

This is important. Funereal is not a synonym for simply "sad" or "unhappy."

Sadness is a broad emotion. You can be sad about a broken toy, a bad grade, or a rainy day. But funereal is a very specific, heavy, formal kind of sadness — the kind that is grave, slow, dark, and almost ceremonially serious. It is sadness with weight. Sadness that presses. Sadness that silences a room.

Similarly, "gloomy" is just dark or pessimistic. "Mournful" expresses grief. "Solemn" means serious. Funereal contains all of these at once — solemn and mournful and gloomy and slow. It is the strongest, most intense version of this family of feelings.
The Three Things Funereal Most Commonly Describes

1. Atmosphere and Mood

The most common use. A place, room, or situation can have a funereal atmosphere — meaning the air itself feels heavy and joyless, like an invisible sadness has settled over everything.

"After the announcement, a funereal silence fell over the office. No one spoke. No one moved."

"The old abandoned house had a funereal quality to it — dark curtains, dim corners, and a stillness that felt like grief."

2. Pace or Movement

Something funereal moves very, very slowly and heavily — the way a funeral procession moves down a street, deliberate and solemn, without any hurry.

"He walked at a funereal pace, dragging his feet as though carrying the weight of the world."

"The negotiations moved at a funereal pace — slow, painful, and exhausting for everyone."

3. Expression, Tone, or Voice

A person's face, voice, or manner can be funereal — meaning deeply grave, dark, and without a trace of lightness or humor.

"She delivered the news in a funereal tone, her voice low and heavy."

"He wore a funereal expression throughout the party, making everyone around him uncomfortable."

Music described as funereal is slow, dark, and deeply solemn — the kind of music that makes your chest feel heavy. Think of a slow, low, minor-key piece that feels like it is mourning something. This is one of the most common uses of the word in writing about art and music.

"The orchestra played a funereal march as the ceremony came to a close."

To sharpen the meaning even further, here is what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean literally connected to a real funeral. You don't describe an actual funeral as "funereal" — that would be odd and circular. The word is used for things that are not funerals but feel like one.
  • It does not mean simply quiet or calm. A library is quiet, but not funereal. A funereal silence has an oppressive sadness to it, not just an absence of noise.
  • It does not mean tragic. Tragedy involves a dramatic, terrible event. Funereal is about the mood and atmosphere that settles in — the gloomy heaviness that follows or surrounds something dark, not the dramatic event itself.
  • It does not mean boring. A dull meeting is not funereal. But a dull meeting where bad news has just been delivered and everyone sits in stunned, heavy silence — that could be funereal.
The Feeling the Word Gives a Reader

When a writer chooses the word funereal, they are doing something deliberate and precise. They are not just saying "things were sad." They are painting a very specific picture: a room, a person, a moment, or a sound that carries the distinctive gravity of death and grief — hushed, slow, dark, heavy, and solemn — even if nobody has died.

It is a word with a lot of weight. When you read it, you should immediately feel a kind of chill — a sense of something pressing and serious. That is exactly what the writer intends.

What it meansHaving the dark, slow, heavy, mournful mood of a funeral
Used forAtmosphere, pace, tone, expression, music
Key feelingOppressive, solemn, hushed, grief-laden
Not the same asSimply sad, gloomy, quiet, or tragic
Typical useDescribing non-funeral things that feel like one
6694: Something is fungible when one unit of it can be swapped for another unit of the same thing, and the swap makes absolutely no difference. Every unit is perfectly interchangeable with every other unit. Nothing is lost, nothing changes — you end up with identical value and function.

The clearest example is cash. Say you have a $10 bill. If a friend swaps it for a different $10 bill, you're in exactly the same position as before. You still have $10. It doesn't matter which specific bill you're holding — they're worth the same, they do the same job, and no sensible person would prefer one over the other. That's fungibility: any one unit can stand in for any other unit of the same type, with zero meaningful difference.

Other classic examples: one barrel of crude oil of the same grade is interchangeable with another barrel. One ounce of pure gold is worth the same as any other ounce of pure gold — if someone owes you an ounce, they can hand you any ounce and the debt is settled. One share of Apple stock is identical in value and rights to any other share of Apple stock.

The concept clicks fastest when you look at what is not fungible.

A house is not fungible. If someone borrows your house and gives you a different house back — even one with the same market value — you are not in the same position. It's in a different location, has a different history, different rooms. The specific identity of the item matters.

A painting is not fungible. The original Mona Lisa cannot be swapped for a perfect replica without something fundamental being lost. A signed baseball from a legendary game cannot be replaced by any ordinary baseball. A specific concert ticket for Seat 12A is not the same as Seat 7C, even if both cost the same.

The test is simple: Does it matter which specific one I get? If yes — not fungible. If no — fungible.
A modern example you've probably heard: NFTs

"NFT" stands for Non-Fungible Token — a digital asset that is unique and cannot be replaced by another. The name itself is built on this word. In contrast, cryptocurrency like Bitcoin is fungible: one Bitcoin is identical in value to any other Bitcoin, so they can be freely exchanged for each other without either party losing anything.
How it's used in real sentences

"Cash is fungible — a dollar is a dollar, no matter which bill you're holding."

"Unlike factory-grade steel bolts, antique hand-forged nails are not fungible; each one is slightly different."

"In large corporations, entry-level workers are often treated as fungible, but a specialist with rare expertise is not."

"The contract specified that the goods were fungible, meaning any equivalent batch of the commodity would fulfill the order."
An important nuance: fungibility can depend on context

Fungibility isn't always a fixed, absolute property of a thing — sometimes context changes it.

A $10 bill is ordinarily fungible. But if it's the first dollar your late grandmother ever handed you, no other $10 bill can replace it. In that personal context, it has become non-fungible — its specific identity now matters to you.

This reveals something important: fungibility is ultimately about whether the parties involved treat the items as interchangeable. In economics and law, things are generally treated as fungible when their units are standardized and indistinguishable by design — like currency, commodities, or identical mass-produced goods. But the moment a particular unit carries unique meaning, history, or attributes that others lack, it crosses into non-fungible territory.

Fungible means perfectly interchangeable — if you can swap one unit for another unit of the same kind and nobody is better off or worse off for it, those things are fungible. If the specific identity of the item matters at all, they are not.
6695: A fungus is a living organism — a life form that is neither a plant, nor an animal, nor a bacterium. It belongs to its own separate kingdom of life, called the Fungi kingdom. The plural of fungus is fungi (pronounced fun-jye or fun-gee), though "funguses" is also acceptable.

Think of a fungus as a living thing that survives by absorbing nutrients from other things — dead wood, soil, food, skin, or even other organisms. Unlike plants, fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight. Unlike animals, they don't hunt or eat. Instead, they release special chemicals called enzymes into whatever they're growing on, break it down, and then soak up the nutrients — almost like digesting food outside their body and then absorbing the result.
What does a fungus look like?

Fungi come in wildly different shapes and sizes, so there isn't one single "look." But most fungi share one structural feature: they are made of thin, thread-like strands called hyphae (singular: hypha). These threads grow and branch out in all directions, forming a tangled web called a mycelium. The mycelium is often hidden — buried in soil, inside rotting wood, or spread through food — and is the main "body" of the fungus doing the work.

What you see above the surface (like a mushroom cap) is not the whole organism — it's just the reproductive part, like a fruit on a tree. The real body is the hidden mycelium underneath.

Some fungi, however, are single-celled and have no visible structure at all — yeasts are a perfect example of this.

Fungi reproduce primarily through spores — tiny, lightweight particles (far smaller than a grain of sand) that are released into the air, water, or soil. When a spore lands in a suitable environment — the right temperature, moisture, and food source — it germinates and grows into a new fungus. This is why mold can appear on bread within days: a few invisible spores landed on it and found exactly what they needed.

Some fungi also reproduce by splitting (in the case of yeast) or by growing new sections from their existing mycelium.

Fungi are found almost everywhere on Earth:

  • In soil — most soil is teeming with fungal mycelium
  • On and inside dead or decaying matter — rotting logs, fallen leaves, old food
  • On living things — on the skin, nails, or inside the body of animals and humans; on the roots or leaves of plants
  • In water — some species live in rivers, lakes, or the ocean
  • In extreme environments — certain fungi survive in deserts, on rocks, and even in radioactive zones

While all fungi share the same basic biology, they vary a great deal in form:

Mushrooms are the most recognizable fungi. The cap-and-stem structure you see is the fruiting body — the spore-producing part. The real organism is the underground mycelium. Some mushrooms are edible (like button mushrooms, shiitake, or portobello), some are medicinal, and some are deadly poisonous.

Molds are multicellular fungi that grow as visible fuzzy or powdery patches — the green or black stuff you see on old bread, fruit, or damp walls. They spread rapidly through spores.

Yeasts are single-celled fungi. They don't form threads or visible structures. They reproduce by budding — a small bud grows off the parent cell and eventually breaks away as a new cell.

Rusts, smuts, and blights are fungi that parasitize plants and cause serious diseases in crops.

Lichens — though technically a partnership between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium — are largely fungal in structure.
The role of fungi in nature

Fungi are among the most important organisms on Earth, primarily because they are decomposers. When a tree falls and dies, when a leaf drops to the ground, when an animal's body is left behind — fungi break it all down. They digest the complex materials (wood, dead tissue, leaves) and return the nutrients locked inside them back to the soil. Without fungi, dead matter would pile up indefinitely and the nutrients inside would never be recycled. In this sense, fungi are essential to the health of every ecosystem on the planet.

Many fungi also form deep partnerships with plants. About 90% of all land plants have fungal networks attached to their roots — a relationship called mycorrhiza. The fungus helps the plant absorb water and minerals from the soil, and in return, the plant shares sugars with the fungus. This partnership is so critical that many plants cannot survive without it.

Beneficial uses:

  • Food: Mushrooms are a major food source worldwide. Yeast is used to make bread rise and to ferment beverages like beer and wine.
  • Medicine: One of the most important antibiotics ever discovered — penicillin — came from a mold called Penicillium. Many other medicines, including immunosuppressants (used after organ transplants), are derived from fungi.
  • Fermentation: Fungi are essential in producing cheese (the blue in blue cheese is a mold), soy sauce, miso, tempeh, and vinegar.
  • Bioremediation: Some fungi can break down pollutants and toxic waste in soil.
  • Research: Yeast has been used extensively as a model organism to study genetics and cell biology.

Harmful effects:

  • Infections in humans: Fungi can infect human skin (athlete's foot, ringworm), nails, hair, mouth (thrush), and in more serious cases, the lungs or bloodstream. These are called fungal infections or mycoses. People with weakened immune systems are especially vulnerable.
  • Crop destruction: Fungi cause enormous damage to agriculture — diseases like wheat rust, potato blight (which caused the Irish Famine in the 1840s), and rice blast devastate crops.
  • Food spoilage: Molds ruin food and can produce toxic chemicals called mycotoxins — like aflatoxin, found in improperly stored grains and nuts, which is one of the most potent natural carcinogens known.
  • Damage to materials: Fungi break down wood, fabric, leather, and even some paints and building materials.

A fungus is a distinct type of living organism — not a plant, not an animal — that feeds by breaking down and absorbing nutrients from other organic matter. Its body is usually a network of microscopic threads called mycelium, spread through soil, wood, or food. It reproduces through spores. Fungi range from microscopic single-celled yeasts to large mushrooms. They play an irreplaceable role in nature as decomposers and as partners to plants. They are also deeply intertwined with human life — giving us food, medicine, and fermented products, while also causing infections, crop diseases, and food spoilage.
6696: "Funk" has a few quite different meanings depending on context. Here they are, one by one.

This is the most common way the word is used today. A funk is a state of feeling emotionally flat, low, and unmotivated — not quite sadness, not quite depression, but somewhere in between. It's that dull, heavy feeling where you don't feel like doing anything, you've lost your usual energy or enthusiasm, and things just feel a bit grey.

The key thing about a funk is that it tends to be temporary and often has no clear reason. It just settles over you. You almost always hear it in the phrase "in a funk":

  • "I've been in a funk all week — I don't know why."
  • "She's been in a bit of a funk since the project fell apart."
  • "He needs to shake himself out of this funk."

Notice that last example — people often speak of "getting out of a funk" or "snapping out of a funk," which tells you it's something you're stuck in temporarily, and the goal is to get through it. It's especially common to talk about creative blocks this way: a writer might say they're in a funk when they can't get any good ideas out.

It's a softer, more casual word than "depression." You wouldn't typically use "funk" to describe a serious mental health condition. It's more like a slump — a period of low energy, low motivation, or low spirits.

A funk can also mean a strong, unpleasant odour — particularly the kind that is stale, musty, sweaty, or stuffy. Think of the smell in a locker room, a room that hasn't been aired out, old shoes, or a gym bag that's been closed for too long. That's a funk.

  • "There's a funk coming from the back of the fridge."
  • "The room had a funk of sweat and old carpet."
  • "His jacket had a funk to it after three days of camping."

This meaning is very common in American English. The smell called a funk is usually not sharp or chemical — it's more of a dull, organic, body-or-mould kind of smell. It's unpleasant but not necessarily dangerous, just... funky.

Funk is also the name of a hugely influential genre of music that was born in African-American culture in the mid-1960s. If you've never heard funk, imagine music built on an irresistibly heavy, rhythmic groove — the kind of beat that almost forces you to move your body.

The defining features of funk music are:

  • A strong, driving beat — often with the drummer hitting very hard on the first beat of the bar (musicians call this "on the one")
  • A deep, prominent bass guitar that dances around in a rhythmic, bouncing pattern
  • Syncopation — meaning the rhythm often hits on unexpected beats, giving it a bouncy, off-kilter feeling that creates tension and release
  • Horns, keyboards, and guitar all playing sharp, clipped, rhythmic parts (not long, flowing melodies — short punchy bursts)
  • A raw, earthy energy — funk is danceable, physical, and deeply rooted in feel over polish

The pioneering figures of funk include James Brown (often called "the Godfather of Soul," his music from the late 1960s is the blueprint for funk), Sly and the Family Stone, and Parliament-Funkadelic (led by George Clinton). Later, Prince became one of the greatest funk musicians of all time.

Funk was a massive influence on nearly every form of popular music that followed. Hip-hop, in particular, is built heavily on sampled funk beats. R&B, disco, neo-soul, and even pop music all carry funk's DNA.

When people say a piece of music "has funk" or "has that funk feeling," they mean it has that deep, irresistible groove — it makes you feel it in your body.

This meaning is largely historical and not common in everyday modern speech, but you may encounter it in older literature or British writing. A funk once meant a state of fear, panic, or extreme anxiety — especially a sudden, cowering kind of fear.

The phrase "a blue funk" was common, meaning a state of terror or nervous panic:

  • "He was in a blue funk before the exam."
  • "The soldier was in a blue funk and couldn't move."

In this sense, it painted a picture of someone paralysed or overwhelmed by fear. You might still encounter "blue funk" occasionally in British English, though it's quite old-fashioned now. In modern usage, this meaning has mostly faded, and "funk" in everyday speech almost always refers to mood or smell (or music).
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "funk" can mean different things, context usually makes it obvious:

  • Talking about someone's feelings or energy? → It's the mood meaning. "She's been in a funk."
  • Talking about a smell, a room, or something physical? → It's the odour meaning. "There's a funk in here."
  • Talking about music, rhythms, or a musical genre? → It's the music meaning. "That song has serious funk."
  • Old text, British literature, or the phrase "blue funk"? → It's the fear meaning.

The adjective form, funky, extends from all these meanings and is worth knowing:

  • Funky smell → has a bad, musty odour
  • Funky music → has that deep groove characteristic of funk
  • Funky style → unconventional, quirky, bold, slightly offbeat in a cool way (this came from the music world — funk was associated with a certain free-spirited, raw aesthetic, and "funky" spread from there to describe anything cool and unconventional)

So when someone says "that's a funky jacket," they almost certainly mean it's interesting, unusual, and stylish — not that it smells. Context, again, is everything.
6697: "Funky" is a surprisingly versatile word. It can be a compliment, a complaint, or a warning — and the same person might use it in all three ways in a single day. Here's every important meaning, explained clearly.
Meaning 1: Having a strong, irresistible musical groove

This is where the word truly lives at its core. Something "funky" has a deep, rhythmic, bass-heavy energy that makes you want to move your body. It comes from funk music — a style built on thick bass lines, tight drum beats, and a syncopated groove that feels both raw and hypnotic.

The key feeling: Funky music doesn't just sound good — it pulls at you physically. Your head starts nodding, your foot starts tapping, almost without you deciding to.

Examples:

  • "This song has a really funky bassline." (The bass is rhythmically rich and groovy.)
  • "James Brown had the funkiest band of his era."
  • "Put on something funky — I want to dance."

You can also use "funky" for non-musical things that carry that same loose, rhythmic, expressive energy:

  • "She has a funky way of walking." (Her walk has a natural, rhythmic swagger to it.)
Meaning 2: Cool in an unconventional, quirky, expressive way

This is probably the most common everyday meaning today. Something "funky" is stylish or interesting, but in a way that's offbeat, bold, and a little unconventional — not in a polished, mainstream way, but in a way that shows personality and creativity.

The key idea: It doesn't follow the rules of normal "pretty" or "elegant." It's eye-catching because it's different, not despite it.

Examples:

  • "She wore a funky hat — bright orange with a wide brim and a feather on it."
  • "That café has funky décor — old bicycles hanging from the ceiling, mismatched chairs, and neon signs."
  • "He has a funky sense of style." (He dresses unusually but with confidence and flair.)
  • "That's a funky idea!" (It's creative, a bit unusual, but interesting.)

Notice that this meaning is almost always positive or neutral. When you call something funky here, you're appreciating its originality.
Meaning 3: Having a strong, unpleasant smell

Here, "funky" shifts completely — it means something smells bad, stale, musty, or just off. Not necessarily rotten or dangerous, but noticeably unpleasant in a way that's hard to ignore.

The key idea: A funky smell is usually damp, musky, or sour — like clothes left wet too long, a room with poor ventilation, old gym shoes, or a cheese that's gone too far.

Examples:

  • "Your gym bag smells funky — please wash it."
  • "There's something funky in the fridge. Check the leftovers."
  • "That basement has a funky odor." (Musty, damp smell.)
  • "My shoes get funky if I wear them without socks."

This meaning is the most direct and literal of the three. There's no ambiguity here — it's clearly a negative observation about smell.
Meaning 4: Something feels wrong, off, or unreliable

When a situation, object, or behavior is described as "funky," it can mean that something seems strange, suspicious, unstable, or not quite right — even if you can't pinpoint exactly what the problem is. It's often used when something raises a vague concern.

The key idea: Your instincts are telling you something is wrong, but you might not have proof yet.

Examples:

  • "Something feels funky about this deal." (It seems suspicious or questionable.)
  • "My laptop is acting funky." (It's behaving strangely — glitching, freezing, doing unexpected things.)
  • "The brakes on this car feel funky." (They don't feel right; something might be wrong with them.)
  • "I don't know, the whole situation seems funky to me." (It feels off or shady.)

This is a very natural, conversational way to express unease without being alarmist.
Meaning 5: Feeling emotionally low or out of sorts (informal, slightly dated)

Less commonly — and more in older or informal usage — someone can "feel funky" to mean they're in a low mood, feeling slightly depressed, or just emotionally not themselves. Not devastated, just... off.

Examples:

  • "I've been feeling funky all week — not sure why."
  • "She seemed funky at the party, like something was bothering her."

This meaning is rarer today and mostly appears in casual conversation. You're less likely to encounter it in writing.
How to tell which meaning is intended

Because "funky" carries such different meanings, context is everything. A few simple rules:

  • If someone is talking about music or dancing → Meaning 1 (groove, rhythm)
  • If someone is talking about style, design, fashion, or ideas → Meaning 2 (quirky-cool)
  • If someone is talking about smell → Meaning 3 (unpleasant odor)
  • If something is not working right or feels suspicious → Meaning 4 (off, strange)
  • If someone is talking about their emotional state → Meaning 5 (low mood)

Example of possible confusion:
"That restaurant was really funky."

This could mean:

  • It had a cool, eccentric vibe and décor (Meaning 2 — a compliment)
  • It smelled bad (Meaning 3 — a complaint)

You'd need the speaker's tone or more context to know which one they meant.
The overall feel of the word

"Funky" is an informal, casual word. You'd say it in conversation, not in formal writing. It has an energy to it — it's expressive and lively. Even when it means something negative (like a bad smell), it doesn't sound harsh. It keeps a certain relaxed, breezy quality.

It's also a word that welcomes emphasis:

  • "That is so funky." (Very stylish.)
  • "Man, this smells funky." (Quite unpleasant.)

And it combines naturally with intensifiers like really, super, pretty, and kinda:

  • "This beat is really funky."
  • "Something kinda funky is going on here."

In short: if "funky" is a compliment, it means something has rhythm, personality, or creative style. If it's a mild complaint, it means something smells, feels, or seems wrong. The difference is almost always clear from context.
6698:
To funnel something means to direct or channel it from a wider, spread-out place into a narrower, more specific path or destination — in a controlled and deliberate way.

Think of the physical object a funnel is: wide and open at the top, narrow at the bottom. When you pour liquid into a funnel, the liquid — no matter how scattered it is at the top — gets guided and concentrated into one single stream at the bottom. The verb "to funnel" borrows exactly this image and applies it to all kinds of things, not just liquids.

Three things are always happening when you use the word "funnel" as a verb:

1. Something is being moved or directed.
There is always a "thing" being funneled — it could be water, air, money, people, information, traffic, energy, resources, or even attention.

2. It is being guided toward a specific place or purpose.
The movement is not random. It goes somewhere — a particular destination, channel, or goal.

3. The act is controlled and deliberate.
Someone or something is causing this directing to happen. It doesn't happen by accident.

In its most direct sense, "funnel" describes physically guiding something through a narrow path or channel.

  • The cave's narrow opening funneled the wind inside, making a loud whistling sound.

(The wind, which was spread out across a wide area, got forced through the narrow gap, concentrating it.)

  • The valley funneled the river toward the sea.

(The shape of the land directed the water into one specific path.)

  • The stadium's single exit funneled thousands of people into one street.

(A large crowd, spread across the stadium, was directed into one narrow passage.)

In each of these cases, notice the pattern: something wide or spread out → gets directed → into something narrower or more specific.
Abstract (Figurative) Use — The More Common Use

This is where "funnel" truly shines, and where you'll encounter it most often. It is used constantly in business, politics, finance, and everyday life to describe directing non-physical things — like money, effort, or information — toward a target.

  • The government funneled billions of dollars into the construction of new hospitals.

(Money from various sources was collected and directed specifically toward that purpose.)

  • All customer complaints are funneled through the support team before reaching the manager.

(Complaints from many different people are channeled through one specific path before going further.)

  • The company funneled its entire marketing budget into social media advertising.

(Resources were concentrated and directed toward one particular area.)

  • The spy was funneling secret information to a foreign government.

(Information was being quietly directed from one place to a specific recipient.)
The Prepositions That Go With It

"Funnel" almost always appears with one of these prepositions, and the choice of preposition slightly shifts the meaning:

  • funnel into → directing something into a destination or purpose
    "They funneled their savings into a new business."*
  • funnel through → directing something through a specific path or process
    "All applications are funneled through the hiring committee."*
  • funnel toward → directing something in the direction of a goal
    "The charity funneled donations toward disaster relief."*
  • funnel to → directing something to a specific recipient
    "The profits were funneled to the company's founders."*
An Important Nuance: The Hint of Secrecy or Manipulation

In many real-world contexts — especially in journalism, politics, and crime — "funnel" carries a subtle suggestion that the directing is being done quietly, indirectly, or in a way that hides the true nature of what's happening. The word doesn't always carry this, but it is a common undertone.

  • "Investigators found that the politician had been funneling public funds into his own accounts."
  • "The drug cartel was funneling cash through fake businesses."

In these cases, "funnel" suggests not just directing, but doing so in a way that avoids scrutiny. This is not the word's only meaning — it can be completely neutral — but if someone says money or information was "funneled" somewhere, it is worth paying attention to whether the context implies something questionable is going on.

To funnel something is to deliberately direct and channel it — from a broader source — into a specific, narrower path, place, or purpose, the same way a physical funnel concentrates scattered liquid into a single stream.
6699:
To furbish something means to clean, polish, or restore it so that it looks bright, fresh, and as good as new again — especially after it has become dull, worn, or neglected over time.

Think of it this way: imagine an old, rusty sword sitting forgotten in a dusty attic for decades. Someone picks it up, scrubs it, polishes it, and works on it until it gleams the way it once did. That person has furbished it.

This word carries two related but distinct uses, and understanding both gives you the complete picture.

1. The Physical, Literal Meaning

In its most direct sense, to furbish something means to physically clean and polish it — to rub, scrub, and shine it until it looks bright and restored. Historically, this was used most often for metal objects: swords, armour, tools, weapons.

The blacksmith furbished the knight's old armour before the ceremony.

The idea is not just cleaning the dirt off — it's about bringing back the original shine and quality that the object once had. You're not just wiping something down; you're genuinely restoring it.

2. The Figurative, Broader Meaning

Over time, the word expanded beyond physical objects. You can also furbish things that aren't tangible — like skills, ideas, writing, or knowledge — meaning you revive, refresh, or update them after they've become rusty or outdated.

After years away from the profession, she furbished her legal knowledge before returning to practice.
The editor furbished the old manuscript, giving it new life for modern readers.

Here, "furbishing" means taking something that has lost its sharpness or relevance and working on it until it's crisp and useful again.

You will very often see this verb paired with the word "up" — furbish up. This is extremely common, arguably even more common than the verb used alone. The meaning stays exactly the same; the "up" simply adds a sense of completion — that the job has been done thoroughly, from a dull or worn state all the way up to a bright, finished one.

He furbished up his old speeches before delivering them to the new audience.
They furbished up the antique cabinet and sold it at a high price.

If you see "furbish up," treat it as one unit meaning: to thoroughly restore something to a fresh, bright, or usable state.
What Kinds of Things Can Be "Furbished"?

This is important for using the word naturally. Things that get furbished are typically things that:

  • Were once good, but have deteriorated — through neglect, age, or lack of use.
  • Have the potential to be restored — they aren't completely ruined, just dull or outdated.

Physical things: weapons, armour, tools, metals, furniture, objects.

Abstract things: skills, knowledge, writing, ideas, arguments, reputation, a speech, one's French, legal know-how.

You would not typically use "furbish" for something being built from scratch, or something completely broken beyond repair. The word specifically implies: something that already existed, fell into a lesser state, and is now being brought back.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

"Furbish" is a formal and somewhat literary word. You are unlikely to hear it in everyday casual conversation. It appears more often in written English — literature, formal essays, historical texts, or careful writing. It carries a slightly old-fashioned, dignified quality, which also makes it feel precise and elegant when used correctly.

It sits in the same neighbourhood as words like refurbish, polish, restore, revamp, and renovate — but it's more specific. Notice that "refurbish" is actually the more common, modern cousin of this word. If you've heard "refurbish" before (as in refurbishing a flat), then "furbish" is essentially the same action, just expressed in an older and somewhat more literary form.
To furbish something is to clean, polish, and restore it — physically or figuratively — so that it recovers the brightness, quality, or usefulness it once had but had lost over time.
